ranked_moves.title: A benchmark Polaris can lose: two plain-session arms (equal reach and full reach), frozen questions and a win rule fixed in advance
ranked_moves.relation: extends P7 (syzygy-fnry.7), which already plans a fresh reader answering frozen questions from the rendered site, and Q13's live scorecard (syzygy-3efd.57). New here: the plain-session arm, the blind grader with a key, the maintainer-documentation ceiling arm, the win rule fixed in advance, and one question file
ranked_moves.prereq: Owner decision, 2026-11-21, in the owner's words: asked what the plain-session arm may read and send, the owner chose 'Everything except detector matches' (the whole clone minus only files the secret detectors match; denied-path and active-content screens are dropped for this arm), over the recommended variant that kept those screens. It applies to this benchmark arm and to public repositories in R16's corpus only; it changes nothing about what a dossier run reads or sends, and no detector is weakened. The equal-reach arm needs no decision. Real runs come from R16's corpus runner after syzygy-k54o.3
ranked_moves.what: For each proving repository, five arms at the same pinned commit: the Polaris dossier; a plain session at equal reach (same model, the screened copy of the clone the author reads, a fixed published prompt and three fixed follow-ups, the same wall-time limit); a plain session at full reach, which is what a user would really get (the whole clone of a public corpus repository minus only the files the unchanged secret detectors match, as the owner decided on 2026-11-21); and the maintainers' own documentation as a ceiling. Before anything is generated, freeze one question file per repository shape: the reader questions, a depth list of ten to twenty non-obvious facts and trade-offs drawn from maintainer documents by a session that sees neither arm, and five reader tasks ('where would I change X'). Fresh readers answer from one arm only; a grader that is not told which arm it holds scores answers against the frozen key; forty sampled claims per arm are checked against the pinned tree. All arms are shown to graders in the same neutral page shell. Record tokens, wall time and operator minutes for every arm. The win rule is written down first: Polaris wins only if its claim error rate is at most half the plain session's, its comprehension and depth scores are not more than ten percent lower, and its cost is within a stated multiple. Anything else is published as a loss, naming the dimension. The three question sets in the repository today (seven in TARGETS, five in the profile, four topics in the brief) become one versioned file that the brief, the reader test and the scorecard all read. Every published result names the arm it was won or lost against: a win at equal reach shows the mechanism helps; only a win at full reach shows an advantage over a real plain session, and the difference between the two arms is what screening costs. Sampled claims are first checked by R2's deterministic checker (resolves, quotation verified, path missing); a model judges only whether a claim matches its cited span, so the claim-error rate rests on Observed checks. Reader tasks are graded against a key of paths taken from the structure record and R19's units, not judged. A figure-ablation measure tags the frozen questions each figure is meant to answer and has fresh readers answer them from the dossier with figures and with figures replaced by their text alternatives; the difference is stored per figure kind, and a kind with no measured gain is listed for R22. A fourth plain arm is budget-matched: the full-reach session given the tokens and wall time the dossier used, with free follow-ups up to that budget, which separates the mechanism from the compute it spends. The aggregation is fixed before the first pass: the number of repositories, a win on at least a stated share of shapes, and no claim from a single repository. Every arm's text is shown to graders as text only, under the source policy's render rule and the no-script rule, because the full-reach arm drops the active-content screen. The owner's decision on that arm is recorded in the owner's words in docs/polaris-generation/BENCHMARK.md by the commit that builds slice 6. The number of sampled claims per arm is set from the error rates the calibration finds, so that the win rule's 'half the error rate' can be resolved; forty is a floor, and a result the sample cannot resolve is published as unresolved. Hold-out: the question file has two parts. The topic questions are public and the author's brief reads them. The graded reader questions, the depth list and the reader tasks are held out: no authoring, inventory, editor or scout session ever receives them, and check asserts their text is absent from every such packet, so the dossier cannot be taught to the test while the plain arm is not. A benchmark pass has its own cost line and budget (sessions per arm, readers, graders), recorded like a run's. A benchmark result never rests on one dossier run: the six stored runs of one commit share 10 of 545 supported-claim clusters, so a single run is one draw. Each corpus repository gets at least two dossier runs and the win rule is applied to the weaker.
ranked_moves.why: The owner's question is comparative, and nothing planned answers it: every existing or planned probe measures a dossier against itself, against pixels or against synthetic shapes. Under the rubric a dimension with no measurement cannot pass 60, and this one instrument also puts numbers on comprehension, claim precision and cost.

[Observed] No run directory holds a reader result. [Inferred] that a plain session wins on speed and reach; its time has not been measured.

ranked_moves.title: Check any synthesis: Syzygy's citation and quotation checker over free-form text
ranked_moves.relation: new; reuses the quotation rule of check and Q3's tally vocabulary; it is the accuracy instrument of R1 and the engine of R15's ask command
ranked_moves.prereq: none
ranked_moves.what: A command that takes any free-form text about a pinned repository (a plain session's answer, an answer to a follow-up question, a pasted design note), extracts every claim that names a path and lines or carries a quoted span, and checks each against the pinned tree with the existing quotation machinery. It reports per claim: quotation verified, reference resolves but is not verified, path missing or quotation not found, or no reference at all, and writes an annotated copy with a tally. The checker measures whether a claim can be checked and whether its quotation is real, not whether an unquoted claim is true; its tally says so, and a count of claims that cannot be checked at all is reported per arm.
ranked_moves.why: It makes the dossier's main advantage visible next to a plain answer: how much of that answer anyone checked. It is also the only mechanical way to score a plain session's accuracy.

ranked_moves.title: Settle coverage before prose: a mechanical coverage pre-check and a coverage plan, so fidelity review judges truth only
ranked_moves.relation: new for the pre-check; its replay over stored runs completes syzygy-fnry.21 (classify why first drafts fail); the plan sharpens Q8's outline (syzygy-3efd.50)
ranked_moves.prereq: none for slice 1
ranked_moves.what: Once the independent inventory exists, `check` lists every inventory entry that no draft block cites near (same path, overlapping lines), by entry identifier and path only, never the entry's text, so the inventory stays independent. The author represents each one or records a justified omission, the same two outcomes the reviewer uses today. Next, Syzygy builds a coverage plan from the inventory: each entry assigned to a page and section, deferred to a deep dive, or omitted with a reason, under the page budget. The author drafts against the plan, check verifies the assignments, and the fidelity review's brief narrows to one question: is each claim true to its citation? Measured 2026-11-21 over the six stored runs: a citation-overlap pre-check would have listed 151 of the 181 inventory entries the first fidelity verdicts marked unsupported (recall 0.83), and 12 of the 184 it lists were entries the reviewer accepted. Both pass the numbers fixed beforehand, so the pre-check is a default step.
ranked_moves.why: Most review failures are bookkeeping, not falsehood, and each one costs a full review round. Removing them is the largest single saving available, and it frees the author's attention for writing.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] fidelity verdicts across six stored runs: 20 not ready of 27. [Observed] of 134 blocking findings, 63 are about inventory coverage and 7 say a cited span does not support its claim (lane scripts over reviews/fidelity-verdict-*.json). [Observed] on first verdicts 20 to 42 of 46 to 66 inventory entries were not represented in five runs. [Observed] newest run: 5 minutes of authoring, about 28 of 34 minutes in review rounds.
slices: S1: overlap advice in check and an author-side justified-omission record; replay over the six stored runs to count what it would have caught
S2: the review step waits until every listed entry has an outcome
S3: the coverage plan record and its check; the fidelity brief narrowed
S4: review rounds per run measured before and after

ranked_moves.title: Never review the same bytes twice: an unchanged-packet stop, review of only what changed, and a labelled fast draft
ranked_moves.relation: sharpens P15 by using the same block digests between review rounds; narrows P1 (syzygy-fnry.1, design-review every checked revision): every revision is still rendered and reviewed, but a page whose rendered bytes are unchanged keeps the verdict reached over those bytes; the fast draft is new
ranked_moves.prereq: stable block identifiers across revisions (present in the draft schema)
ranked_moves.what: Three rules. A review is not dispatched when its packet digest equals the previous round's; the record says the previous verdict stands. After the first round a fidelity packet carries only blocks whose text, citations or label changed, the inventory entries still open, and the previous round's open findings; unchanged supported blocks carry their verdict forward with the digest it was reached over, and a full re-review runs every third round so carried verdicts cannot drift. A design packet after the first round carries only pages whose rendered bytes changed, plus the landing page. Separately, a fast mode: one author session, the deterministic layers and check, no inventory and no review, with a banner on every page that says so, a tally showing nothing reviewed, and no way to promote it except a full re-run. A fast draft never enters the corpus, the benchmark arms or the human panel. Carried verdicts are counted, and each third-round full review reports how often it disagreed with a carried verdict, as a drift figure. Measured 2026-11-21: none of 16 later fidelity deliveries had the same packet digest as the one before, so the unchanged-packet stop would not have fired once; it stays as a guard, not a saving. Unchanged items are 30 percent of later packets' canonical bytes and 20 percent of their file bytes, at the edge of the 30 percent fixed beforehand: delta packets are built as an option and become default only if the first corpus pass shows fewer review minutes, not fewer bytes.
ranked_moves.why: Whole review rounds have bought nothing, and every round pays for the whole draft. A review binds to bytes, so carrying a verdict by digest is honest. An owner looking at a new repository often wants its shape in minutes, and an honest label makes that safe.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] consecutive identical fidelity verdicts five times across four runs. [Observed] fidelity packets stay 348 to 413 KB within the newest run and design packets are 3.1 to 5.2 MB each (lane script review_economy.py). [Observed] packages/polaris-dossier/src/review-packet.ts builds a whole packet every round.
slices: S1: the unchanged-packet stop
S2: fidelity packets of changed blocks with carried verdict rows and a full re-review every third round
S3: design packets by rendered page digest
S4: the fast mode, its banner and its record flag

ranked_moves.title: An editor session fenced by check, and house style taught by example
ranked_moves.relation: new for the operator-agent loop: it ports the Edit stage that only the parked provider pipeline has; pairs with R5 (review only changed blocks)
ranked_moves.prereq: none
ranked_moves.what: After the first draft passes check, a fresh editor session gets the draft, the rendered pages and the house style. It never gets the repository. It returns changes to wording, order within a section, and merging or splitting of blocks. Check refuses any change to a citation, label, quotation, judgement mark, figure element or Unknown, by comparing each block's claim ledger before and after, and advises when a rewrite introduces an identifier or number not in the block's cited spans. The author accepts or rejects each change. House style becomes a versioned data file of twelve to twenty before-and-after pairs over a fictional project, each tagged with the habit it fixes; the author's and editor's briefs carry the pairs in place of the prose rules now spread over two parts of the brief, which shortens the brief. The ledger check cannot see a rewording that changes meaning, so every block the editor changed goes to the fidelity review as a changed block; no edited block keeps a carried verdict.
ranked_moves.why: One session cannot hold 4,910 words of rules about evidence and also write well. A separate editor can only change how claims read, never what they claim, because check fences it, so voice can improve without risk to truth. Models follow examples more reliably than abstract rules.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] the newest brief is 4,910 words; 170 are about voice and 711 about citation, quotation and labelling (lane script over brief.md). [Observed] packages/polaris-dossier/src/brief.ts:54: voice rules are open to no mechanical check. [Observed] session roles are author, inventory and review only (packages/polaris-dossier/src/session-handover.ts); docs/polaris-generation/AUTHORING.md:122-128 defines an Edit stage for the provider pipeline alone.
slices: S1: the claim-ledger equality check between two revisions
S2: the editor brief and change format, run by hand on the stored newest draft and measured with R7's ledger
S3: twelve exemplar pairs replacing the overlapping brief rules
S4: the editor as a step of the loop, with per-change acceptance
S5: a house-style version is compared through R1 before it becomes the default

ranked_moves.what: A quotation the project states becomes its own element: a pull quote set with its file and lines as attribution, attached to the sentence it supports. The formula 'The project states:' leaves the prose; the author writes its own sentence and attaches the quotation as support, and check still verifies the span. Each section gains a one-sentence thesis the renderer sets as its opening. Each run stores model-free prose measures per page (sentence-length spread, apparatus phrases, quotation lead-ins, identifiers per hundred words, whether the opening is an answer, examples and numbers per section, counts of judgements and worth-knowing marks). ranked_moves.title: Ask for insight by name: worth-knowing marks, comparison under a label, and length earned by evidence
ranked_moves.relation: extends P8 (syzygy-fnry.8, a cited judgement per Pole) with comparison under a label and the worth-knowing mark; changes the length rules that Q8's depths and Q10's size tiers make safe to change
ranked_moves.prereq: none from the owner: under VIS-4 as amended by D10 this is an agent adoption, recorded as a row in AGENT-ADOPTIONS.md with its revert command; the owner may veto it. The present rule (a comparison only as quotation) was the owner's trade-off; the adoption row says so and names what changes. Q8's depth slice comes before the length change
ranked_moves.what: Three changes to what the author is asked for. Each Pole carries one to three blocks marked worth knowing: a cited fact an engineer new to the project would not guess from its category, shown as a distinct callout near the top; the inventory session gets the same request, so missing ones surface as coverage gaps. A labelled judgement may compare the project's choice with a named, widely known alternative when it cites the project's own mechanism as its premise and marks the alternative's property as general knowledge and Inferred; it renders as a 'Compared with' aside and never as the maintainers' claim. The flat limits of 300 words per section and three deep dives give way to budgets the evidence earns: a deep dive for each mechanism whose blocks cite at least eight distinct spans in two files, capped by the repository's size tier, and section length that scales with supported claims; check advises a Pole with fewer than three choices or trade-offs on record. The benchmark's depth list is drawn not only from maintainer prose but also from the derived tables (what the tests pin down, deprecations, changelog reasons) and, where admitted, history (hidden coupling, the oldest unchanged core). A Pole with no fact that meets the worth-knowing test says 'none found'; the one-to-three request is a ceiling with a reason required for zero, not a quota.
ranked_moves.why: Depth comes from naming the non-obvious, and nothing in the brief asks for it. 'Why this and not the obvious alternative' is the insight a newcomer most wants and a plain session gives freely; forbidding it outright costs depth without buying truth, because the label already carries the state. The limits were a cure for an overlong overview that reading depths now solve.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] packages/polaris-dossier/src/brief.ts:72-73: a comparison only as quotation, never an alternative of the author's own, and an unstated advantage never written even as Inferred. [Observed] :88-89: 300 words per section, three deep dives. [Observed] the newest draft holds 0 Inferred blocks and 0 judgements; its understanding record holds 1 choice, 1 trade-off and 1 limit for all of Redis; it wrote one deep dive. [Observed] run 3 counted 0 judgements across seven drafts.

S2: the comparison rule adopted with its row, its fidelity instruction and the aside
S3: the advice floor for choices and trade-offs per Pole
S4: earned deep dives and section budgets, after reading depths exist

ranked_moves.relation: new derived content for Q2's structure record and Q9's pack recognizers. Slice 3 builds run 4's retained tag-and-changelog timeline idea. The scout sharpens P10

ranked_moves.what: Three deterministic harvests over admitted files, each a derived table. Test names per framework, mapped to units: a Pole shows 'what the tests pin down' and the author may cite a test name as evidence that a behaviour is intended. Markers: TODO, FIXME, deprecation notices and issue references, each a verified line, giving per-unit counts and a 'rough edges and what is going away' page; an issue reference is Observed as a reference and its content is Unknown, because trackers are outside the clone. ranked_moves.title: History as its own screened class: churn, age and hidden coupling derived; commit messages screened as content
ranked_moves.relation: builds run 4's retained full-history idea (and run 3's history mining) by splitting metadata from message content
ranked_moves.prereq: none from the owner: under VIS-4 as amended by D10 this is an agent adoption, recorded as a row in AGENT-ADOPTIONS.md with its revert command; the owner may veto it, because acquisition form and classification are screening policy within SEC-5. Two limits keep it there: commit messages pass the unchanged secret detectors and fail closed, and author identity is dropped at ingestion and never stored. A successor source policy and a change to the acquisition form carry it
ranked_moves.what: Two levels. Metadata only: a history fetch bounded by count or date keeps commit identifiers, dates, parent links and changed paths, and drops author identity and message text at ingestion. From it Syzygy derives churn per unit, age of last change, an age for every cited span ('unchanged since 2019'), and pairs of files that change together yet share no declared or import link, drawn as a hidden-coupling figure. Messages: commit message text becomes a content class that passes the same secret screening as files; the author may quote a message that states a reason, verified like any quotation, and must label any reading of it Inferred. Authorship stays out of both levels. Identity is dropped wherever it appears: author and committer fields, and message trailers that name people (signed-off-by, co-authored-by, reviewed-by and the like) are removed before a message is stored. A quoted commit message is also screened for people: a span containing an e-mail address or an @-handle is not quotable. Names in running text cannot be removed reliably, so messages are stored only as the spans an author quotes, never whole.
ranked_moves.why: Where a project is still moving, what is stable, which parts are secretly entangled, and why a design changed: no reading of the current tree can give these, and they are what a senior engineer tells a newcomer first.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] packages/polaris-dossier/src/clone-shape.ts:20: the clone holds exactly the pinned commit. [Observed] no production module reads commits, messages or blame. [Observed] .syzygy/governance/policies/POLARIS-DOSSIER-DECLARED-SOURCE-POLICY-v1.json:79-80 lists work-history as never classified. [Inferred] the size of the gain: no dossier has ever cited history.

S2: age on each citation; a per-file timeline on source pages

ranked_moves.title: One surface made by one hand: role-named tokens with a lint, colour with two jobs, one shape vocabulary, and a specimen sitting
ranked_moves.relation: extends Q6's figure kinds and Q7's element types with one shape vocabulary; legend generation is Q3 slice 1's (syzygy-3efd.17) and is reused, not rebuilt; builds run 3's retained type-scale idea; new: the token module, the lint and the specimen sitting
ranked_moves.prereq: none to build slices 1 to 4. R12's composition is built once, against the bar's default token set; the owner's sitting (slice 5) can then change tokens only, never the composition, so neither waits for the other
ranked_moves.what: One module owns every dossier style value by role: a modular type scale, line heights, a four-pixel spacing grid, a reading measure, two radii, and colour roles. Nothing is named after a hue or a typeface. The stylesheet is generated from it, and a test fails on any size, colour or spacing that is not a token. One panel style is kept for figures; emphasis elsewhere uses weight and a rule, not a box. Colour does two jobs only: which Pole something belongs to, and its evidence state; colour by list position goes. Every figure kind draws from one shape vocabulary keyed by element type (a store is a cylinder, an external system a dashed frame), and each figure's legend is generated from the shapes it uses. Taste is settled once: the renderer produces a specimen (the stored Redis overview and one Pole) in three token sets that differ only in typeface pairing, scale ratio, default theme and accent family, the owner picks one in a single sitting, and the pick becomes the default. The specimen sitting comes before the first screen is composed (R12), so composition is done once against the chosen tokens. At the sitting the owner is also asked to name two or three existing documentation sites as the reference bar.
ranked_moves.why: A document is trusted on sight when it looks made by one hand. Today's sheet is a stack of fixes that cannot stay consistent, and each review round produces new spacing notes. A single sitting spends the owner's taste where only the owner can decide and nowhere else.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] 23 distinct font sizes in three units, 7 radii and 31 one-pixel borders in the dossier stylesheet (lane script over the newest site). ranked_moves.title: Polaris makes its own evidence: an agent-started corpus of public repositories, run on every mechanism version
ranked_moves.relation: new; makes real the live corpus of Q13 (syzygy-3efd.57) and the generality probe (syzygy-fnry.22), which both wait for runs only the owner could start before D10
ranked_moves.prereq: `syzygy polaris <url>` runs with no record (syzygy-k54o.3) and R3's stage budgets (slice 3). An agent adoption: which repositories are read, which provider receives them and unattended work are agent-decided; observed code is never executed
ranked_moves.what: A fixed, versioned corpus of public repositories, each pinned to a commit and chosen to cover the space, not for convenience: at least one repository per trait the shape packs declare and per size tier of the scale ladder, including a large monorepo, an infrastructure-only repository and a data- or documentation-only one; a synthetic private-visibility fixture covers what public repositories cannot. A runner starts a dossier run for each, unattended, under the declared source policy. A pass is due only when the mechanism version changes, and that version is a digest over the brief, schema, check and renderer modules, so a cosmetic commit triggers nothing. Each pass has a total token and wall-time budget on top of R3's stage budgets; shapes it does not reach are recorded Unknown. A generality pass rule is written before the first pass: every shape reaches a reviewed close within budget, and no shape scores below the full-reach plain arm on more than one dimension. Failures are recorded results. Each run feeds R1's arms, Q13's scorecard and the reading, prose and cost ledgers. The corpus also holds a repository whose documentation is not in English and one with no README or documentation root. Each run records which traits matched no shape pack and which units the scale ladder left derived-only, so a generality failure is a named gap and not a quietly thin dossier. The scorecard has a row for figure coverage against the figure policy (required views present, omitted with a reason, missing) and a depth row per Pole (cited choices, trade-offs and limits, worth-knowing marks, top-ten coverage). The pass rule states minimums for those rows and cost targets: a ceiling on median tokens, wall time and review rounds per dossier, and a refresh target for R14 (at most a third of a full run when under ten percent of cited spans changed). On each pass a fixed number of known-false blocks (a wrong line range, an inverted claim, an unsupported number) are seeded into one copy of a review packet and the fidelity reviewer's recall is recorded; below a stated recall the pass's readiness verdicts read 'uncalibrated'. The seeded copy never enters a dossier. The private stratum is not only synthetic: it includes repositories the owner owns (the owned-repositories list), read under the same policy. The cost targets are numbers, fixed from the first recorded baseline before the second pass: median wall time and tokens per dossier at most 0.7 of the baseline median, median review rounds at most three. Each repository is run at least twice per pass. The cost baseline is the six stored runs' medians, which exist today, not a baseline the plan chooses later. Every dossier states on its review page that it is one draw and, where replicate runs exist, how far they agree.
ranked_moves.why: Every real dossier so far is of one repository, and every planned real-repository measure waited for the owner to start a run by hand. Since D10 that wait is no longer required. Without this, generality and the benchmark stay claims.

ranked_moves.relation: New sources and a new required topic. It extends R9's harvest machinery and run-4 Q9's packs (the call-name lists are pack data). The 'bite you' judgements use R8's labelled comparison and P8's premise rule. It also feeds R19: assertion density is a salience signal.

ranked_moves.what:
Three more deterministic harvests, each producing a derived table of verified lines, run over admitted files by the R9 machinery.
(1) Invariants: assertion calls per language, matched lexically from a closed versioned list (`assert`, `serverAssert`-style project macros detected by an `*assert*` call-name rule, `debug_assert!`, `invariant(`, `precondition(`, `require(` in Kotlin, `Debug.Assert`). Each row is a verified line, grouped by unit.
(2) Failure surface: string literals passed to error-returning, panic and log-at-error or warn calls (the call names are pack data), plus error-code enums. Each becomes a row: message, path, line, unit.
(3) Limits and defaults: entries of a documented configuration file (`*.conf`, `config.example.*`, `values.yaml`, `settings.py` defaults, CLI flag definitions), and named constants matching `*_MAX*|*_LIMIT*|*_THRESHOLD*|*_TIMEOUT*|DEFAULT_*`, each with its literal value.
The brief gains a required topic, 'Operating envelope: what is always true, what fails and how, where it gets slow'. Its parts:
- a failure-mode table per major mechanism (trigger, what the code does, what the user sees), each row citing harvested lines;
- a 'cliffs' list of thresholds where behaviour or cost changes, each citing the constant or config default;
- 'three things that will bite you': labelled judgements whose premises are harvested rows.
The inventory session gets the same topic, so a missing failure mode becomes a coverage gap. Where a language has no call-name list, or a harvest finds nothing, the topic shows a named Unknown for that language and kind, never an empty table. Each 'will bite you' judgement needs at least two harvested premises of different kinds (for example a limit and a failure message). The harvests' precision is measured on fixtures with known answers, not only their recall. Where nothing is found, the topic says 'none found' with the harvest's coverage; a quota is never filled with weak rows.
ranked_moves.why: This is what a senior maintainer says in the first hour and no planned source yields. Tests say what is intended, markers say what is unfinished and release notes say what changed; none says what must never happen, what the error looks like, or which default to raise. All three are exact, cheap, language-general harvests. Every row is Observed, so the topic adds depth without loosening truth.

ranked_moves.title: Measure now on the six stored runs: variance, a pooled ceiling, replays and reviewer consistency
ranked_moves.relation: New measurements over existing stores. (c) is R4 S1's replay made a stated metric pair. (d) quantifies R5. (b) gives the review-score-3 gap 'the ceiling arm is never acted on' a stand-in today. (a) is new and may justify a pooled-author move (R28).

ranked_moves.what:
A read-only analysis script over the stored run directories, never `run-*.agents/` or `run-*.sessions/`, writing one evidence record that names each subject's digest (rule 11). It reports six figures.
(a) Author variance at fixed input: the cited-path overlap measured here, extended to claim level (blocks whose cited spans overlap) and to Pole and thesis agreement across runs.
(b) A pooled pseudo-ceiling: the union of supported claims and inventory entries across six runs, and each run's share of it. This gives a depth-headroom number before any maintainer-ceiling arm exists.
(c) R4 replay: for each first fidelity verdict, the share of entries the reviewer marked unsupported that the citation-overlap pre-check would have listed (recall), and how many it lists that the reviewer accepted (noise).
(d) R5 replay: rounds and packet bytes the unchanged-packet stop and delta packets would have saved, computed from the stored packet digests and block digests.
(e) Reviewer consistency: for consecutive verdicts over packets with equal digests, whether the readiness and finding sets agree.
(f) Stage time per review round from steps.jsonl, with the operator minutes R21's fault asks the cost line to count.
Optionally, local renders of the stored sites in the existing headless browser give R12's first-screen pixel facts (title lines, hero above the fold, horizontal scroll at 390 px). This needs no provider. Decision numbers are fixed before the results are read: R28's two-author mode is built only if a second fresh run at the same brief adds at least 25 percent more supported-claim clusters to the first; R4's pre-check becomes a default step only if its recall on first-verdict omissions is at least 60 percent with noise under 30 percent; R5's delta packets become default only if they would have saved at least 30 percent of packet bytes after round one. The pooled figure is reported at several clustering thresholds, because the choice of when two claims count as the same inflates or shrinks the union. First results, 2026-11-21 (six runs of one commit, brief versions 1 to 7): a run holds 14 to 51 percent of 545 pooled supported-claim clusters and 10 clusters are in all six; under a loose match (any overlapping cited span) 79 percent of a run's blocks have a counterpart in another run, under a strict one 32 percent, so the size of the variance depends on the rule; three runs have no Poles; review rounds take 57 percent of 302 wall minutes; five re-submitted verdicts over identical packets agree on readiness every time.
ranked_moves.why: The reviewer says the last points need measurement and that k54o.3 gates the corpus. These figures need neither: they turn R4's and R5's planned savings and R1's depth gap into measured baselines now, and author variance is a finding the plan does not yet have. If one run cites half of what six cite together, then 'regenerate and pool' or 'two authors, merged' may earn more depth than any brief change. That decision should be made from this number.

dimensions.name: Truth: every claim's evidence state is honest and checkable
dimensions.reason: The strongest dimension, and already real: citations and quotations re-derived from Git objects, Observed reserved for what Syzygy verifies. The plan adds derived facts with receipts (Q3), a generated legend and tally, honest close (P1), a free-text claim checker (R2), staleness against a newer commit (R14, R20) and a 40-claim audit per arm (R1). Held under 90 by four things: whether a cited span supports its claim is still judged by a model reviewer and nothing measures that reviewer's false-accept rate; R8 admits comparisons whose second half is 'Inferred general knowledge' with no checkable link; R5 carries verdicts forward and adds an unreviewed fast mode; R6 lets an editor reword claims whose citations stay byte-equal.

dimensions.name: Comprehension: a newcomer understands the system fast
dimensions.reason: Thesis and spine (P3), reader routes (P4), page shape and reading depths (Q8), walks (Q5), a running example (Q14), an editor (R6), a composed first screen (R12), and three planned measures (P7 probe, R1 benchmark, R21 people). That is a complete design. It is not higher because the plan's own win rule only asks that comprehension be 'not more than ten percent lower' than a plain session until the third corpus pass, the human sample is at most three readers, and every mechanism depends on author sessions that have produced 0 judgements and one trade-off in six runs.

dimensions.reason: Typed kinds (Q6), one model with views (Q7), hero figure (Q4), click-to-source and walks without script (Q5), a figure policy (Q12), derived arrows (Q3), one shape vocabulary (R11). Measured by figure lint and the transcription probe (Q11). The gap is in the rubric's own words: nothing measures whether a figure carries explanation. The transcription probe measures whether a figure can be read back, not whether it taught anything; R1 has no arm with the figures removed. Eight hand-built layouts with no script is also the largest single build risk in the plan.

It is not higher because six to nine repositories is not 'any', the only private case is synthetic, recognizers are capped at three structured formats and four test frameworks so an unrecognized ecosystem falls back to today's path with no stated degradation rule, Q1 waits on an owner answer, and R16 waits on syzygy-k54o.3. All six real runs today are of one repository.

dimensions.name: Depth of insight: the why, the trade-offs, the non-obvious
dimensions.reason: Worth-knowing blocks and labelled comparison (R8), harvests of tests, markers and release notes (R9), history as a class (R10), importance ranking (R19), decision cards (P8). Measured by R1's depth list. Three limits: the depth list is drawn from maintainer documents, so it rewards restating what the docs already say and cannot credit an insight the docs lack; issues and pull-request discussion, which the run brief named as the place the why lives, are read by no move; nothing reads code semantically (call graphs and tree-sitter parsing are retained, not ranked), so 'non-obvious' stays whatever an author session notices.

Tokens and lints buy consistency, which is necessary and is not beauty. No move names a visual reference the surface is held to, the one taste decision (the specimen sitting) is optional, and the main beauty measure is a model reader's taste, which the plan itself labels Inferred.

dimensions.name: Measured advantage over a vanilla LLM session
dimensions.reason: The measurement design is good: four arms, a frozen question file, a blind grader, a win rule written first, losses published and turned into repairs (R1, R2, R18, R21, R22). The dimension asks for a measured advantage and the plan holds none; its own lanes expect the plain session to win on speed, reach and follow-up. Further deductions: the accuracy instrument (R2) checks only claims that name a path or quote a span, so it measures citability more than truth and treats the two arms asymmetrically; forty claims per arm on three repositories cannot support 'at most half the error rate'; citations and labels unblind the grader; the plain arm is a fixed prompt plus three fixed follow-ups, which is not how a person uses an agentic session.

dimensions.name: Economy and lifecycle: cost, time, freshness, follow-up
dimensions.reason: Recorded cost and stage budgets (R3), coverage settled before review (R4), no repeated review (R5), refresh and a 'since' page (R14), a staleness stamp (R20), index, task routes and ask (R15), print and bundle (R13). Measured by R3. Not higher because no cost or time target is stated anywhere ('within a stated multiple' has no number), the plan adds an editor, scouts, corpus passes and benchmark arms, the claim that R4 and R5 save more than those add is Inferred, whether the agent tool exposes token use is Unknown, and follow-up is an operator command: a reader of the static pages still cannot ask anything.

substantial_improvement.answer: Yes as a durable, checkable artifact; unproven as an explanation; no on speed, cost and follow-up.
why_yes: A plain session's synthesis is unverifiable prose that vanishes with the session. The built product is a persistent multi-page site in which every claim carries a state and a resolvable link, figures say which arrows were derived and which are readings, coverage is stated against a denominator, and a newer commit marks which claims went stale. A plain session offers none of these and cannot be made to by prompting.
It is the only one of the two that says what it did not read.
why_not_yet: On whether a newcomer understands faster or learns more of the why, the plan promises a measurement, not a result, and its own win rule accepts up to ten percent worse than a plain session on both for the first two passes.

A plain agentic session answers in minutes, reads everything, and takes any follow-up. The dossier takes 30 to 81 minutes today, several sessions, and answers follow-ups only through an operator command.
The honest sentence for the owner: substantially more trustworthy and more lasting, very probably better looking, and not yet shown to be better understood.

units.gap: The surface is calm, legible and accessible: a warm off-white or warm charcoal ground, one sans stack, a 1.7 line height, measured columns (60-90ch), and checked contrast in both themes. It is not yet a designed object. It reads as a stack of fixes, each correct alone and never composed. On the 1440x900 first screen a reader sees a full-bleed status banner flush to the window edge, a 37-word provenance paragraph, a six-item legend box, an eyebrow, and a three-line 70px title that hyphen-breaks 'in-memory'. The first sentence of the thesis arrives near the fold, and no figure is on screen. On a Pole page the first screen holds no content at all, only a parent link, a 70px title, a '03' eyebrow and an H2. The type system has no scale: the inline CSS sets 23 distinct font sizes in three units (em, rem, px) and 7 corner radii, and draws 31 one-pixel borders. The font token still named --font-serif is defined three times in one stylesheet, ending as a sans stack. Callouts, figures, cards, details, notices and the legend all draw the same bordered rounded panel, so nothing leads and everything is a box. There is no print stylesheet and no visual identity: nothing marks the site as Polaris or as about Redis beyond the title. Run 4 made the figures correct. The surface around them now needs one owner with one system: scale, rhythm, a hero, and fewer boxes.

units.gap: A dossier costs 30 to 81 minutes of wall time from first prompt to last step across six stored runs. It uses four model sessions (author, inventory, fidelity, design), three to seven draft revisions, and about a dozen operator touches. Its token cost is unknown because usage is self-reported at close and was not recorded on the newest run. Fidelity review is where the time goes. Across all stored verdicts it returned not-ready 20 of 27 times (the brief's 18 of 23 excludes one run), and the newest run spent 26 of its 34 minutes in review rounds. The leading cause is coverage bookkeeping, not falsehood: 63 of 134 blocking fidelity findings are about the understanding record, an inventory entry not represented or its omission not justified, and the reviews logged 428 'unsupported' inventory dispositions. The draft is asked to represent every inventory entry while keeping each section to about 300 words, and the reviewer enforces the first. Only 7 blocking findings say a claim is not supported by its citation and 4 say a claim overstates. Most of the cost buys completeness against a list. The rest is operator ceremony: three terminals to start, a launch-form answer for each, a fresh-session decision for each repair round, and usage figures typed at close. A vanilla session needs none of these.

units.gap: The author reaches the surface of a repository and is barred from most of the places the 'why' lives. On the newest Redis run the draft carries 293 citations into 20 files. Four files (redis.conf, README.md, src/server.c, MANIFESTO) hold 212 of them (72%). The understanding record holds one choice, one trade-off and one limit for all of Redis. Three structural limits cap depth regardless of model quality. History: the clone holds one commit, nothing in Syzygy reads commits, and the policy lists work-history as never classified, so a design's origin, a reversal or a rationale in a commit message cannot be cited. Tests: 300 test files sit in the pinned tree, and the author excluded tests/ as 'not needed', with no rule asking otherwise. The 300-word section cap and the three-deep-dive cap then bound what little is found (the newest draft wrote one deep dive). Code comments are reachable and cited (src/*.c), and the release notes are cited 10 times, so rationale in those two forms does get through.

units.gap: A dossier is a sealed artifact with no life after close. It is a directory of 42 static HTML pages under the operator's state root, opened as files. The dossier command family 'serves no route and opens no socket', and its sixteen commands all end at close. After that nothing refreshes, compares, answers, searches, exports or links back. When the repository moves, the only path is a new run from preflight, with nothing carried over: no previous draft, inventory, verdicts or citations. This run's economy figures show what a refresh costs: 30 to 81 minutes and a dozen operator touches, the same as the first dossier. Nothing says which claims a new commit changed. The changed-source regeneration in TARGETS (Redis 7.2.4 to 7.4.0 to 8.0.0, the licence change) is the right proof, and it is unrun. A reader with a follow-up question ('where do I change eviction?', 'why is this config default?') has no way in: the pages carry no search, no question entry, and no route from a task to the files that matter, though the source pages already know which files each claim rests on. Sharing depends on someone deciding to expose the state root. Printing has no stylesheet (beauty unit). The one piece of lifecycle that works is provenance: every page carries the pinned commit and packet digest, so a reader can tell exactly which revision a page describes.

units.gap: The prose is accurate, flat and readable at sentence level, but it reads like a compliance document. The brief spends its words on what may be claimed, not on how to write. Voice gets 170 of 4,910 words (3.5%). Citation, quotation and labelling rules get 711 (14.5%). No voice rule is checked mechanically. The output follows the rules: the introduction leads with the category ('an in-memory key-value store') and walks one command end to end, and the best section opening states a trade-off ('Redis buys speed by running commands in memory… and pays for it in durability'). But three habits the rules force or allow drag every page. First, every stated advantage arrives in one formula, 'The project states: "…"', nine times, and the author then splices its own next claim onto the quotation, which makes the longest sentences (63, 49 and 42 words). Second, the draft carries 0 Inferred blocks and 0 judgements, so there is no authorial voice, no 'this matters because', and no view on which ideas are central. Third, the first section reopens with the introduction's sentence. The prose bar asks for one idea per sentence and examples before abstractions; 14 of 107 sentences run past 30 words, and the draft names 'for example' or 'such as' 10 times in 2,272 words.

units.gap: Across the six run-5 units, three systemic causes recur. (1) One session is asked to do every job at once. A single author holds 4,910 words of brief, 85% of it about what may be claimed, and must explore, cover every inventory entry, stay under 300 words per section, and write well. Fidelity review then judges truth and coverage bookkeeping together. Result: flat, formula-bound prose (prose), one choice and one trade-off for all of Redis (insight-depth), and 20 of 27 fidelity verdicts not-ready, mostly over coverage (economy). (2) The rules guard against error by forbidding whole kinds of content rather than by labelling them. History is never classified, comparisons may only be quoted, and an unstated advantage is forbidden even as Inferred. The labels that doctrine already provides (Inferred, judgement) go unused, at 0 and 0 in the newest draft. This buys truth at the cost of the 'why' a newcomer wants and a vanilla session supplies freely. (3) Nothing is measured against anything outside the dossier. There is no vanilla arm, no stored reader result, no token cost, no run-over-run ledger, no first-screen assertion and no CSS census, so dimensions 5 to 8 cannot score above 60 under the rubric however good the work is. The single change that moves the most rubric weight is V1+V2, the paired vanilla arm with a blind four-axis scorecard. It lifts the 60 cap on dimension 7 directly and puts numbers on 2 (comprehension), 1 (claim precision) and 8 (cost) using one instrument. It also turns every other move in this run into a measurable bet rather than a judgement. It is cheap relative to its reach because the reader-test port, frozen questions and reference sites already exist. The highest-leverage build move after it is E1 (coverage plan before prose), which removes most review rounds and frees the author to write.

units.gap: Nothing in the repository can compare a dossier with a plain session today. The reader-test engine exists but has one implementation, a scripted port that returns answers fixed in advance, and it records accuracy as 'not-evaluated'. No reader result, scripted or real, is stored for any run. The three question sets in play disagree: TARGETS has seven frozen questions, the profile five, and the brief four topics. The planned probes measure a dossier against itself (P7 grades against fidelity-confirmed claims and the inventory) or against pixels (P6, Q11); TARGETS adds a reader of the maintainers' own site, but none has a plain-LLM arm. So 'a substantial improvement over vanilla sessions' is an unmeasured claim, and under the rubric dimension 7 cannot score above 60. Fairly stated: the dossier author already is a vanilla session (Claude Code, Opus) that may read the whole clone. What the dossier adds is a harness: a pinned revision, Git-verified citations and quotations, explicit Unknowns, two independent reviews, screening, and a durable multi-page site. What it takes away is reach (citable set narrowed by policy), interactivity (no follow-up), latitude (fixed topics, 300-word sections, three deep dives) and time (34 minutes of wall time plus operator steps on the newest run). A fair test has to let each side show its strength.

proposals.title: A pre-registered vanilla-arm benchmark that Polaris can lose
proposals.what: Three arms per repository: (A) a Polaris dossier; (B) one plain session with the same model, clone, sandbox and wall-clock cap, given a fixed published prompt ('Explain this repository to a newly hired engineer: why it exists, how it works, its key trade-offs; include diagrams as Mermaid') and three fixed scripted follow-ups; (C) the maintainers' own site, as a ceiling. Before any generation, freeze per repository: the seven TARGETS questions; a depth rubric of 10-20 non-obvious facts and trade-offs drawn from maintainer docs, ADRs and changelogs by a session that never sees A or B (CodeWikiBench-style); and five reader tasks ('where would I change X'). Measurements: (1) claim accuracy, sampling 40 claims per arm, each judged by a verifier session holding the clone with the arm identity hidden, plus V2's mechanical check on any file:line either arm gives; (2) comprehension, with fresh readers answering the frozen questions from the rendered arm only, graded against the frozen key; (3) depth, as rubric items covered; (4) task success; (5) figures, as count plus the run-4 pixel round-trip; (6) cost: tokens, wall time, operator minutes. Blinding: both arms are rendered to the same neutral HTML shell, with Polaris's apparatus folded and B's file references kept, so graders see content, not chrome. Pre-registered win rule: Polaris wins only if its accuracy error rate is at most half of B's AND its comprehension and depth scores are not lower by more than 10% AND its cost is within a stated multiple (proposed: 10x tokens, 5x wall time). Anything else is published as a loss, with the dimensions named.
proposals.why: Rubric dimension 7 cannot score above 60 without a measurement, and the owner's question ('a substantial improvement over vanilla sessions?') has no answer today. Making the loss condition explicit is what makes a win mean something (VIS-1: truth first, including about Polaris itself).

proposals.what: A `dossier-tokens.ts` module owns every dossier value by role: text sizes on a modular scale (a ratio of about 1.2 from a 17-18px body: caption, small, body, lead, h3, h2, h1, display), line heights per size, a 4px spacing grid, a 66-72ch measure, radius and stroke tokens, and colour roles (ink, muted, surface, raised, line, accent, focus, the epistemic three, Pole hues). proposals.title: A mechanical coverage pre-check before fidelity: name the inventory entries the draft never touches
proposals.what: Once the inventory has run, `check` computes, for each inventory entry, whether any draft claim block cites a span that overlaps that entry's cited spans (same path, overlapping line range), or names the entry's path. Entries with no overlap are listed to the author as advice, by entry id and path only: 'inventory entry inv-23 (src/aof.c:1210-1288) has no draft block citing it'. The entry's claim text is never shown, so the author must read the source and decide, which keeps the inventory independent. The author represents each entry or records a justified omission, the same dispositions the reviewer uses. Fidelity then reviews a draft whose obvious coverage gaps are already closed. The pre-check never sets readiness; the reviewer still judges coverage.
proposals.why: Coverage omissions are the largest repeated cause of not-ready verdicts, and a citation overlap catches most of them for nothing. Each avoided fidelity round saves a review of 280 to 770 KB plus an author revision. It also moves the 'unsupported' counts on first verdicts (38/66 typical) toward the 12/92 the best run reached.
proposals.basis: VIS-2 (a gap shown, never hidden); the independence of the inventory session is preserved because only ids and paths cross

proposals.title: Review only what changed, and never review the same bytes twice
proposals.what: Two rules. (1) A packet digest gate: the supervisor refuses to dispatch a review whose packet digest equals the previous round's, and records 'unchanged, previous verdict stands'. (2) Delta packets: after round 0, a fidelity packet carries the blocks whose text, citations or label changed (keyed by block id and its content digest), the inventory entries whose disposition was open, and the previous verdict's open findings. Unchanged supported blocks carry forward their 'supported' verdict with the digest it was reached over, and the verdict file records which rows were carried and from which round. A design packet after round 0 carries only pages whose rendered bytes changed, plus the landing page always. A full re-review happens on demand or every Nth round (proposed: 3), so carry-forward cannot drift indefinitely.
proposals.why: Five consecutive identical verdicts mean whole rounds bought nothing. Packets that stay at 90-100% of their first size mean every round pays for the whole draft. Delta review is the standard incremental-build move, and digest-keyed carry-forward keeps it honest under rule 10 (a review binds to bytes).
proposals.basis: VIS-2 and the rule-10 discipline already used across the repository: a verdict is bound to the bytes it read, so a carried verdict names its digest

proposals.what: Fast mode: one author session, the deterministic layers (census, run-4's derived structure, W1-W3 tables) and `check`, but no inventory and no reviews. proposals.title: The operating envelope: invariants, failure modes and cliffs, harvested and then explained
proposals.what:
Three more deterministic harvests, each producing a derived table of verified lines, run over admitted files by the R9 machinery.
(1) Invariants: assertion calls per language, matched lexically from a closed versioned list (`assert`, `serverAssert`-style project macros detected by an `*assert*` call-name rule, `debug_assert!`, `invariant(`, `precondition(`, `require(` in Kotlin, `Debug.Assert`). Each row is a verified line, grouped by unit.
(2) Failure surface: string literals passed to error-returning, panic and log-at-error or warn calls (the call names are pack data), plus error-code enums. Each becomes a row: message, path, line, unit.
(3) Limits and defaults: entries of a documented configuration file (`*.conf`, `config.example.*`, `values.yaml`, `settings.py` defaults, CLI flag definitions), and named constants matching `*_MAX*|*_LIMIT*|*_THRESHOLD*|*_TIMEOUT*|DEFAULT_*`, each with its literal value.
The brief gains a required topic, 'Operating envelope: what is always true, what fails and how, where it gets slow'. Its parts:
- a failure-mode table per major mechanism (trigger, what the code does, what the user sees), each row citing harvested lines;
- a 'cliffs' list of thresholds where behaviour or cost changes, each citing the constant or config default;
- 'three things that will bite you': labelled judgements whose premises are harvested rows.
The inventory session gets the same topic, so a missing failure mode becomes a coverage gap.
proposals.why: This is what a senior maintainer says in the first hour and no planned source yields. Tests say what is intended, markers say what is unfinished and release notes say what changed; none says what must never happen, what the error looks like, or which default to raise. All three are exact, cheap, language-general harvests. Every row is Observed, so the topic adds depth without loosening truth.

proposals.title: Pages that hold attention: a figure that stays while the text walks through it, sidenotes, and a one-page edition
proposals.what:
Three static, script-free forms.
(1) Sticky-figure sections: on a wide screen, a mechanism section is a two-column grid. The figure sits in one column with `position: sticky`, and the numbered steps scroll in the other. Each step names the numbered callout it explains, and the matching figure region carries the same number in the Pole hue. The view stays fixed while the explanation moves, which is the core move of the best interactive explainers, done in CSS. Below the measure width it falls back to figure-then-steps.
(2) Sidenotes: citations, definitions on first use and short asides move into a margin column on wide screens (CSS grid, the Tufte layout), and inline toggles open them on narrow screens. The prose column carries only prose. This replaces inline apparatus in place, with no extra page.
(3) The one-page edition: a single designed page, landscape A3 in print and a long single screen on the web, assembled only from elements already checked. It holds the thesis, the hero figure, each Pole's one-line answer with a thumbnail of its figure, key numbers from the derived tally, the three 'bite you' judgements (F1) and 'where to start' links. It makes no new model claims. It is rendered by the C1 tokens, and its PDF gets a digest beside R13's.

proposals.title: Measure now on the six stored runs: variance, a pooled ceiling, replays and reviewer consistency
proposals.what:
A read-only analysis script over the stored run directories, never `run-*.agents/` or `run-*.sessions/`, writing one evidence record that names each subject's digest (rule 11). It reports six figures.
(a) Author variance at fixed input: the cited-path overlap measured here, extended to claim level (blocks whose cited spans overlap) and to Pole and thesis agreement across runs.
(b) A pooled pseudo-ceiling: the union of supported claims and inventory entries across six runs, and each run's share of it. This gives a depth-headroom number before any maintainer-ceiling arm exists.
(c) R4 replay: for each first fidelity verdict, the share of entries the reviewer marked unsupported that the citation-overlap pre-check would have listed (recall), and how many it lists that the reviewer accepted (noise).
(d) R5 replay: rounds and packet bytes the unchanged-packet stop and delta packets would have saved, computed from the stored packet digests and block digests.
(e) Reviewer consistency: for consecutive verdicts over packets with equal digests, whether the readiness and finding sets agree.

Run 3's P15 (regeneration and claim diff) is the engine for the first. units.framing: A newcomer can get the what from the code. A manifesto's value is the why: why this design, what it replaced, what it costs, what is fragile, what is on its way out. That knowledge sits in places the dossier never reads: tests (intent the maintainers made executable), release notes and changelogs (decisions in time order), in-code markers (TODO, FIXME, deprecations, issue references), and git history (churn, age, files that change together, commit messages). The lens sorts these by what Syzygy can derive deterministically as Observed (names, counts, dates, co-change), what it can verify as a quotation (Observed text whose meaning is the author's Inferred reading), and what needs a new acquisition or a new content class. History is the one that needs an owner decision.

A Pole page gets a 'What the tests pin down' strip: the 5-8 test names whose words overlap that Pole's glossary terms, each linking to its line, plus a count ('214 tests cover the persistence unit'). proposals.title: History as its own consented class: churn, age and hidden coupling derived as Observed; commit messages screened as content
proposals.what: There are two acquisition levels. Level H1, metadata only: a history fetch bounded by count or date (for example the last 2,000 commits or 3 years) that keeps commit ids, dates, parent links and changed paths, and drops author identity and message bodies at ingestion. From it Syzygy derives churn per file and unit, last-change age, a co-change matrix (pairs of files that change together more than a stated threshold and share no derived import or manifest edge, the 'hidden coupling' figure), and an age per cited span (each citation shows 'unchanged since 2019-04'). All of these are counts and dates over git objects, so they are Observed by derivation. Level H2, commit messages: message bodies become a content class that runs through the same secret screening as files. The author may quote a message that states a reason, verified like any quotation, and must label any reading of it Inferred. Authorship stays out of both levels unless the owner decides otherwise.
proposals.why: Churn, age and coupling are the non-obvious facts no reading of the current tree can give: where the project is still moving, what is stable, which parts are secretly entangled. Commit messages are the richest rationale source in most repositories. Rubric dimension 5 gains most here.
proposals.basis: Observed by derivation under trust-and-evidence's own definition, so no doctrine change. It does stretch the spec-level acquisition form (one commit, clone-shape.ts:20) and adds a content class. Under D10 that makes it an owner question on two counts: commit messages can carry secrets, and authorship is personal data. [Inferred: if the owner reads SEC-2 consent as covering only the tree at the pinned commit, this becomes vision-extending and needs a SEC-2 amendment.]

units.framing: The measurement surprised this lens. Sentence mechanics are no longer the problem. In the newest Redis draft sentences average 16.7 words (p90 27), hedges and passives are rare, every section opens with an answer, and apparatus fell from 57 phrases to 10 between run d9411d26 and the newest run 658f2f90. A mechanical style checker would mostly confirm what is already fine, and would teach the author to write to it. What the prose lacks is substance and voice: 2,100 words for all of Redis, zero judgements, and no sentence a senior engineer would underline as 'I didn't know that'. So this lens spends its moves on asking for insight, editing as a separate act, and style taught by example. Metrics stay descriptive and out of the author's sight.

proposals.title: An editor session: one fresh reader-writer who reads the checked draft as an argument and returns block diffs
proposals.what: After the first draft passes `check`, and before the fidelity review, a fresh editor session receives the draft, the rendered pages (or P6 screenshots once they exist), the house style (VO2) and the prose ledger (VO4). It never receives the clone. It returns a block-level diff: rewritten text for blocks, reordering within a section, and merges or splits of blocks. It may not change any citation, label, quotation span, judgement mark, figure element or Unknown. `check` refuses a diff that does, mechanically, by comparing every claim block's citation set, label and quotation list before and after. It also refuses a rewrite that introduces a new identifier or number absent from the block's cited spans; this is lexical and advisory at first. The author then accepts or rejects each diff hunk, and the result is a new draft revision. Fidelity reviews only rewritten blocks (economy E2).
proposals.why: Writing and editing are different jobs. The author spends its attention on evidence, so the prose is correct but flat. A separate editor can only improve how claims read, never what they claim, because the check fences it. This is the cheapest route to voice that cannot cost truth.

proposals.title: House style as data: exemplar pairs, not more rules
proposals.what: A versioned `house-style.json` of 12-20 before-and-after pairs, each tagged with the habit it fixes: apparatus ('Every entry here is the project's own wording, quoted from its files' becomes a direct claim); claim-first ('X buys A by B and pays for it in C'); hand-off causality ('so that …'); naming the alternative a design rejects, when the sources name it; one concrete number or example per abstraction; and a judgement with its premise. Pairs are Syzygy-written and project-neutral, built over a fictional project, so a brief carries no other project's content and no copyrighted prose. The author brief and the editor brief (VO1) carry them in place of the prose habits currently spread across VOICE_RULES and READABILITY_GUIDANCE. That trims the brief rather than adding to it. The V1 benchmark A/B-tests a house-style version before it becomes the default.
proposals.why: Models imitate examples far more reliably than they follow abstract rules, and today's voice guidance is numbered rules spread across two blocks of brief text (brief.ts:55-61 and :82-90). Keeping style as data makes it versioned, reviewable and testable, like run-4's shape packs.

proposals.title: Ask for insight by name: a 'worth knowing' mark per Pole
proposals.what: The brief asks each Pole for one to three blocks marked `worthKnowing: true`: a cited fact a competent engineer new to this project would not guess from its category alone. Examples of the shape: 'writes are durable only after the next fsync, by default once a second', or 'the event loop is single-threaded, but I/O threads parse and write'. They render as a distinct 'Worth knowing' callout near the top of the Pole. `check` counts them as advice. The V1 benchmark's frozen depth rubric scores whether they match what maintainers and experts flag. The independent inventory session gets the same request, so 'worth knowing' items the draft lacks show up as coverage gaps, as other inventory entries do.
proposals.why: Depth does not come from longer prose. It comes from naming the non-obvious, and nothing in today's brief asks for it. Making it a marked element gives readers the thing vanilla sessions do well (a sharp 'gotcha') and gives the benchmark a population to score.

proposals.title: A prose ledger that describes and never gates, kept out of the author's sight
proposals.what: Each run stores the model-free prose metrics per page and per section: the sentence-length distribution, hedge and passive rates, apparatus phrases, quotation lead-ins, identifier density, opening-is-an-answer (first sentence declarative and free of apparatus), concreteness (numbers, code excerpts and examples per section), and counts of judgements and worth-knowing blocks. The ledger is shown on the review report, diffed against the previous run of the same repository, and handed to the editor session (VO1) and the design reviewer. It is never in `check` output to the author, and it never sets readiness. Only extreme outliers raise a design-review prompt: p90 over 35 words, or more than 3 apparatus phrases per 1,000 words.
proposals.why: Metrics are useful to see trends (the apparatus collapse above was invisible until measured) and dangerous as targets. Keeping them out of the author loop is the 'avoid writing to the checker' rule made structural.
proposals.basis: VIS-2 (measure what is known); AUTHORING.md 'neither a word quota nor an exhaustive catalog is the objective'
